Trump says there is ‘positive momentum’ towards ending the war on Iran following a ceasefire proposal delivered by Qatar

SOURCE 2 (Al-Monitor) :
Trump sees 'positive momentum' on Iran after Qatar PM talks
US President Donald Trump said on Monday there was "positive momentum" toward ending the war with Iran after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House.
"I had an excellent conversation with Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani," Trump said on Truth Social, adding that "much was discussed with respect to the Islamic Republic of Iran."
The meeting with the Qatari prime minister -- a key mediator in the Iran war -- is Trump's first with a foreign leader since his party's massive losses in the midterm elections.
In the weeks leading up to the vote, there was widespread speculation that US strikes against Iran would resume soon after.
However, Trump has talked down resuming the conflict while leaving the door open to further strikes.
In his post on Monday, Trump reiterated that the US was "locked and loaded," but that he believed further strikes were "quite unlikely" given that key US allies in the Gulf "would prefer the status quo."
"We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America's interests are at all times protected," Trump said.
Trump's comments echoed early statements to CNN over the weekend when he said it was "highly unlikely" fighting would resume.
- 'Imaginary talks' -
Iranian officials meanwhile expressed defiance at the continued pressure from Washington.
The Islamic republic's top security chief, Mohsen Rezai, wrote on X late Monday that the US "flails like a desperate gambler," telling Washington to "fold your hand. Stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks."
Earlier, Tehran's top negotiator Mahammad Bagher Ghalibaf claimed on X that Israel was pushing the US deeper into conflict, adding that "unless Washington drops the 'Israel First' mindset, America and its allies are headed straight for a dark age."
On the ground in Iran, strikes -- which have not been publicly acknowledged by the US military -- are continuing, according to Iranian authorities.
The island of Qeshm, located in the Strait of Hormuz, was targeted overnight from Sunday to Monday, the provincial deputy governor stated on state television.
Trump has acknowledged that the highly unpopular war with Iran was at least partially responsible for the Republicans' defeat, not least because it has contributed to rising prices in the US economy.

SOURCE 1 (Al Jazeera) :
Negotiators from Russia and Ukraine are set to meet for peace talks brokered by the United States in Abu Dhabi, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that recent gains on the battlefield had strengthened his country’s hand.
The meeting in the capital of the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday will be the third round of talks there this year, following security consultations in January and February. The US side is led by US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded Washington’s mediation.
The three delegations last met in Geneva on February 18.
“Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating position,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was “suffering record losses”, a claim Moscow disputes, and urged Washington to persuade the Kremlin to end the war.
Zelenskyy said General Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented a report on Ukraine’s military positions that pointed to heavy recent Russian losses, and that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including oil facilities, were having an effect.
“We are responding to Russia’s war in a fully justified manner and demonstrating that this war must end,” he said. “Russia can do this. It can end its war. It is important that the United States convince Russia of precisely this.”
‘Strong inclination’
In Washington, DC, Trump told reporters that he saw a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.
“We’re having a very good conversation about that in Abu Dhabi,” he said.
Trump had promised to end the war quickly when he took office in January 2025, but a settlement has remained elusive nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
A US official, briefing reporters on the condition of anonymity, said on Monday that both Russia and Ukraine had privately shown some flexibility on a possible exchange of territory. Security guarantees for Ukraine would be a central topic, the official said, including the possibility of a defence commitment modelled on Article 5 of NATO’s founding treaty.
Both Ukraine and Russia have been adamant about territory.
Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to obtain all of the Donbas region.
Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea and parts of the eastern Donbas region. The Russian move has not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has previously urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war.
The US official said any territorial agreement would most likely come at the end of the negotiations, once other issues, including a post-war security framework, had been settled.
‘Ways to go’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio meanwhile struck a cautious note, saying that the process to end the war still has “a ways to go”.
“We’ll keep trying. And that’s what we’ve been trying to do the whole time is try to be creative and find ways that we can help bring that conflict and that war to an end,” Rubio said.
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, will again lead the country’s delegation, according to The Kyiv Independent. Russia’s team will be headed by Vladimir Medinsky, a Kremlin aide, and will include Sergei Ryabkov, a deputy foreign minister, as well as Yuri Zhigarlovsky, a senior military officer.
European powers, including France, Germany and the European Commission, will send officials to the talks in Abu Dhabi, but Russia has made it clear it doesn’t want the Europeans to take part in negotiations.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said the talks would focus on security guarantees. European officials would not take part, he added, because the negotiations had been agreed to as a three-way format.
“What will take place in Abu Dhabi in the coming days is trilateral negotiations between Russia and Ukraine with US mediation,” Peskov said. “As for the presence of Europeans, you know that the Americans have their own channels of communication with Europeans, and Ukrainians with Europeans.”

ABSTRACT
Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the 
lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest 
social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian 
villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much 
a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-
assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal 
social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community 
ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of 
neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best 
target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community 
targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed

“The distinctive characteristic of a problem of social policy is indeed the fact that

1. Introduction
Most social programs are intended to be targeted to the ‘neediest,’ but it is not
necessarily clear what that means. Is the relevant target the household with the
lowest level of consumption or the one who will benefit the most from the transfer?
And when we consider who will benefit the most, whose point of view do we have in
mind? For example, even parents often have a different view of consumption options
for their children than the children themselves. Might communities feel the same way
about their members? While a libertarian might say that the community’s views are
irrelevant, the community might want a say.
In this paper, we argue that these distinctions are largely ignored in current policy
practice, based on the assumption that they are more or less the same. Yet they
represent fundamentally different normative stances. We develop a framework that
allows us to probe these issues and their implications for the choice of targeting meth-
ods, and examine them empirically. We use unique data that we collected from over
5,500 villagers in Indonesia, which asks each respondent not only about their con-
sumption and their self-reported well-being, but also about who in their community
has the lowest level of welfare, and crucially, who will be assisted the most by a social
transfer. Our survey shows these notions of need are distinct. An RCT covering 600
villages shows which notions different targeting methods reflect in practice.
There is a reason why these concerns are not more salient in discussions about
targeting. The standard framework assumes a social planner who allocates benefits
to maximize a utilitarian aggregate social welfare function under the assumption that
while households may be richer or poorer, their preferences are the same. Specifically,
suppose that each household i has a utility function u(ci,1,ci,2,...,c i,n) of different
consumption choices cij, increasing in each good j and jointly concave, which they
maximize subject to budget constraint ∑ jcij =Ci. This generates a concave indirect
utility functionU(Ci). The utilitarian social maximand is ∑ iU(Ci+di), wheredi = 1
if the household gets a small government benefit and 0 otherwise. This tells us that
the benefits should be targeted to those with the highest U′(Ci). Under the standard
assumption that U is identical across households and concave, those with the largest
U′(Ci) are the same as those with the lowest U(Ci), and are also the same as those

concern for the worst off, despite their different rationales (Rawls, 1971). 1

one person to another. The first empirical finding of this paper is that this does not
seem to be true. In our survey, we solicited both household consumption Ci and self-
assessed welfare Ui(Ci).2 When we compare self-reported welfare with consumption
at the household level, we find that higher consumption often does not imply higher
well-being. Although they co-move, the raw correlation is only 0.33. As such, very

clear that once we have this type of heterogeneity, it is no longer obvious that one
should necessarily target the poorest. 3

6. Discussion
Targeting as a Normative Choice. Targeting requires a normative objective.
Who is “neediest” depends on whether the planner prioritizes low consumption ( Ci),
low self-assessed welfare (Ui(Ci)), low community-assessed welfare in levels (Vi(Ci)),
or a large community-assessed gain from the transfer ( V′ i (Ci)). These rankings do
not have to agree, and different targeting methods build in different notions of need-
iness. A consumption-based rule is justified by a benchmark in which households are
exchangeable at the margin conditional on consumption. An ordeal ranks households
by private net willingness to participate. This corresponds with marginal utility only
when the costs of the ordeal do not overturn the private-benefit ordering; otherwise
it corresponds to valuing households less should they happen to have higher costs
to perform the ordeal (e.g., disability, social exclusion). Community targeting likely
reflects both socially assessed welfare in levels and assessed gain from the transfer.
These distinctions matter empirically. Targeting the bottom decile of consumption
misses 77% of the households with the highest community-assessed gain from the
transfer. Evaluating a PMT against consumption is thus not equivalent to evaluating
it against the community’s social-gain ranking. None of this implies that the com-
munity ranking should bind the planner. While a community ranking may combine
local information about debt, dependency, and vulnerability, it is also possible that
it incorporates likely uses of the transfer and other social judgments that the planner
may not endorse, though we do not see evidence for this in our context. More gen-
erally, a policymaker needs to be clear about their normative stance, whatever it is:
which components of local social valuation they are willing to incorporate, and why.
The choice must be purposeful, not an accident of the targeting method. Our MSV-
PMT illustrates one strategy that could potentially be used to predict high marginal
social valuation for targeting. However, it also has tradeoffs: it places more weight
on the community’s marginal social valuation ranking than a standard PMT trained
to predict consumption, but fails to completely reproduce direct elicitation, showing
that unobservables play a major role in a local society’s normative perspective.
Implications for Impact and Algorithmic Targeting. These distinctions extend
to recent work studying how targeting should trade off baseline deprivation against
heterogeneous impacts (Haushofer et al., 2025; Bj¨ orkegren et al., 2026). Related evi-
dence on poverty traps and general-equilibrium spillovers shows why the effects of an
antipoverty intervention may be persistent, heterogeneous, and extend beyond direct

tion. If the planner trades impact against deprivation, the approach is cardinal. Let

planner may have some∂Cϕi(Ci,zi)ti. Note that while ti are painstakingly estimated

choice of welfare metric as on the precision with which ti is estimated.
The issue is not that this literature fails to specify welfare criteria. Haushofer
et al. (2025) explicitly vary the welfare function, curvature, outcome, time horizon,
and Pareto weights. Bj¨ orkegren et al. (2026) separate heterogeneous impacts from
welfare weights on people and weights on outcomes. Egger et al. (2022) likewise

choice of welfare criterion (e.g., homogeneous CARA/CRRA utility) embeds an aspect

A set of cash transfer experiments in Kenya illustrates the problem. Haushofer
et al. (2025) find that the households predicted to have the largest consumption ef-
fects are not the most deprived. But in the same setting, Walker et al. (2025) find
that nearly the entire reduction in infant mortality is concentrated among very poor
households, and that mortality effects are essentially zero among groups predicted to
have the largest consumption and asset gains. This suggests that instead of map-
ping everything to consumption, as is done in practice, there is a vector of effects
that ought to be normatively considered. “Targeting impact” is incomplete until
the researcher specifies which effects count and how they are aggregated. Clearly
a one-dimensional consumption index can reweight consumption gains by baseline
consumption, but it cannot independently value child survival, disability, or vulner-
ability. (But our empirical V′ i is deliberately reduced form and permits respondents
to integrate whichever consequences they regard as relevant. It neither separately
identifies those consequences nor the weights placed on them, nor is it intended to.)

Recent innovations in prediction methods do not escape these normative issues.
Aiken et al. (2025) compare proxy means tests, community nominations, and machine-
learning predictions based on mobile-phone metadata. Their comparison defines suc-
cess relative to consumption poverty. The PMT reproduces that target most accu-
rately, while phone-based targeting can be more cost-effective under some combina-
tions of program scale, screening costs, and transfer budgets. Though these findings
establish which mechanism best implements the consumption target, as we have ar-

shows that analogous prediction machinery can instead be trained on V′ i directly,
though unobservables limit how far this goes. There is also a question of portability.
Perhaps it is reasonable to think that a function predicting consumption is stable
across communities, but who is to say that social valuations or moral judgments are?
The issue is also not one of scaling. Algorithms scale nicely, clearly, provided the
prediction function is stable – though there is a serious question of quality of pre-

touch than a PMT. But it need not be prohibitively expensive. In this same exper-
iment, community targeting was cheaper to administer than a scaled PMT (Alatas
et al., 2016b). And it has the advantage of potentially targeting a socially valued
goal.45 There is a bit of a blind spot at times in the literature about this trade-off.
Concluding Remarks. When a government writes down a targeting rule, it is im-
plicitly maximizing some normative objective. The policymaker’s own normative
view may or may not align with the objective being implemented – perhaps naively,
or perhaps as a deliberate second best 46 – but it is important to be clear, because it
clarifies the kind of policy one wants. Normative perspectives will also differ and, re-
specting some boundaries, there is scope for pluralism without unbounded relativism.
Communities, for instance, hold normative views of their own: they assess who gains
from a transfer, possibly in complex ways that line up with neither welfare levels nor
private preferences, and a non-paternalistic policymaker may at least want to con-
sider those assessments. We have shown that these distinctions matter empirically
and that the standard targeting methods implement different ones. Prescriptively,
then, a policymaker must be clear about what their normative goal is, because that

limited data, what problems to solve, and which counterfactuals to engage.

Working Paper Series 
Unlocking supervisory effectiveness in 
credit risk: insights from the ECB’s 
supervisory findings and measures 
Alessandra Agati, Adele Fontana, 
João Matos Leite, Claudia Schwarz 
Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB. 
No 3308 / November 2026 
 
 
Abstract 
This paper provides an assessment of supervisory effectiveness in credit risk using confidential 
data from ECB Banking Supervision. The analysis covers 8,106 supervisory measures issued 
and closed between 2016 and 2025. A central contribution is the constr uction of a measure-
level indicator of supervisory effectiveness based on large language model (LLM) analysis of 
supervisory narratives and closure justifications. The indicator captures whether supervisory 
measures resulted in full remediation of the underlying deficiencies. Using logistic and duration 
models, we examine the characteristics of findings, measures, and banks associated with 
remediation outcomes and remediation speed. The results show that multi-faceted findings are 
a key driver of supervisory outcomes. Measures related to data, reporting, and IT deficiencies 
are less likely to achieve full remediation and require longer remediation periods. Measures 
originating from on -site inspections are associated with higher remediation rates and faster 
closure. Stronger governance is also associated with more successful remediation outcomes. 
 
 
Keywords: supervisory effectiveness, credit risk, large language models, banking 
supervision 
JEL classifications: G21, E51, H81, G28 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
1
Non-technical summary 
Effective banking supervision requires more than identifying weaknesses in banks. It also 
requires ensuring that banks address those weaknesses in a timely and comprehensive 
manner. Yet assessing whether supervisory actions actually lead to remediation rem ains 
challenging. Supervisory performance is often measured through completed processes and 
activities, while evidence on whether supervisory interventions resolve the underlying 
deficiencies is much more limited. 
This paper provides new evidence on supervisory effectiveness in the area of credit risk using 
confidential data from ECB Banking Supervision. The analysis is based on more than 8,100 
supervisory measures issued and closed between 2016 and 2025 and recorded in the ECB's 
Findings and Measures database. The paper focuses on whether supervisory measures 
achieved their intended objective, namely the remediation of the deficiencies identified by 
supervisors. 
A key challenge is that remediation outcomes are not directly recorded in structured 
supervisory data. Although a measure may be formally closed, closure does not necessarily 
imply that the underlying issue has been fully resolved. To address this challeng e, the paper 
applies large language models (LLMs) to supervisory narratives and closure justifications to 
classify measures according to whether they resulted in full, partial, or no remediation. This 
creates a novel outcome -based indicator of supervisory effectiveness that can be analysed 
systematically across a large number of supervisory cases. 
Using this indicator, the paper examines which characteristics of supervisory measures, 
findings, and banks are associated with successful remediation and the time required to 
achieve it. 
The results show that supervisory effectiveness differs substantially across both measure 
types and institutions. 
First, the complexity of the underlying finding is an important determinant of outcomes. 
Measures addressing multiple issues are less likely to achieve full remediation and take longer 
to close. Similarly, deficiencies related to data, reporting and IT systems are among the most 
difficult to remediate, both in terms of success rates and remediation time. This reflects the 
substantial organisational, technological, and operational changes often required to address 
such weaknesses. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
2
 
 
Second, measures originating from on -site inspections are associated with more successful 
and faster remediation than measures resulting from broader supervisory processes such as 
the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) or ongoing supervisory monitoring. 
This finding suggests that highly targeted and in-depth supervisory assessments can facilitate 
corrective action and highlights the importance of using different supervisory tools in a 
complementary manner. 
Third, more severe supervisory measures are less likely to achieve full remediation and 
generally remain open for longer periods. This likely reflects the fact that more severe findings 
are often associated with deeper -rooted weaknesses and require more ex tensive corrective 
action. 
Fourth, bank characteristics matter, although their influence is generally weaker than that of 
finding and measure characteristics. Banks with stronger governance frameworks and those 
with higher profitability tend to achieve higher remediation rates . However, some of these 
relationships become less pronounced once differences across supervisory teams and 
institutions are taken into account, suggesting that remediation outcomes are influenced by a 
combination of bank-specific and supervisory factors. 
The results have several implications for supervisory authorities. They highlight the importance 
of designing supervisory measures that are sufficiently focused, clearly communicated, and 
tailored to the nature of the underlying deficiency. They also point to the particular challenges 
posed by complex, cross-cutting issues, especially those involving data and IT infrastructures, 
where remediation may require longer time horizons and sustained supervisory follow -up. 
More generally, the results can support supervisors in allocating resources and calibrating 
supervisory intensity more effectively. 
Beyond the substantive findings, the paper demonstrates how artificial intelligence can support 
supervisory effectiveness assessments. By transforming large volumes of unstructured 
supervisory information into structured data, LLMs make it possible to eval uate supervisory 
outcomes at a level of granularity that would otherwise be difficult to achieve. While the results 
should be interpreted as evidence of associations rather than causal effects, they provide a 
new and practical framework for monitoring and analysing supervisory effectiveness in banking 
supervision. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
3
 
 
1. Introduction 
The Global Financial Crisis and subsequent episodes of banking stress highlighted the 
importance of effective banking supervision and triggered far -reaching reforms of regulatory 
and supervisory frameworks. These reforms included revisions to the Capital Requi rements 
Directive and Capital Requirements Regulation, as well as the establishment of the Single 
Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in 2014 under the auspices of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). More recently, the banking turmoil of March 2023 renewed attention on the role of 
supervision in identifying vulnerabilities and ensuring that banks address them in a timely 
manner. 
But what defines effective supervision, and how can it be assessed? The Basel Committee on 
Banking Supervision (BCBS, 2025) defines supervisory effectiveness as: “Effective 
supervision promotes the safety and soundness of banks and the banking system by promptly 
assessing prudential risks, identifying material shortcomings within banks, and using the 
supervisory toolkit and powers appropriately to ensure that banks remediate shortcomings in 
a timely manner.” Effectiveness extends beyond compliance, focusing on timely intervention, 
corrective action, and institutional resilience. The BCBS identifies two key purposes for 
assessing supervision: public accountability and optimi sing supervisory strategy, such as 
determining which tools to use for different banks and how to allocate resources. Crucially, 
effectiveness should be measured by outcomes, not just outputs, as what matters is whether 
a bank’s remedial actions resolve identified shortcomings. 
Importantly, supervisory effectiveness should not be equated with changes in observed risk 
metrics. Supervisory measures rarely seek to reduce a specific level of credit risk directly. 
Instead, they typically aim to address weaknesses in governance arrange ments, risk -
management processes, internal controls, methodologies, data quality, reporting frameworks, 
or other prudential deficiencies. Consequently, a supervisory measure should be considered 
effective when the bank successfully implements the required corrective actions and 
remediates the identified shortcoming. In fact, effective supervision may sometimes lead to a 
temporary increase in measured risk if improved methodologies, controls, or reporting 
practices result in more accurate risk identification. For this reason, the focus of this paper is 
on remediation outcomes rather than subsequent changes in credit risk indicators or prudential 
metrics. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
4
 
 
Despite a growing literature on supervisory effectiveness, evidence on supervisory outcomes 
remains limited. Existing studies typically evaluate supervisory tools by examining their impact 
on bank behaviour, lending activity, risk-taking, or market outcomes. While these approaches 
provide valuable insights, they do not address a more granular question: whether individual 
supervisory measures achieve the remediation of the specific deficiencies they were intended 
to correct. Answering this question has prove d difficult because the relevant information is 
rarely available in structured datasets and often remains embedded in confidential supervisory 
documentation. 
This paper addresses that gap using confidential data from ECB Banking Supervision's 
Findings and Measures (F&M) database. The database contains detailed information on 
supervisory findings and measures generated through on-site inspections, horizontal reviews, 
ongoing supervisory activities, and the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP). 
Although the database contains more than 75,000 observations since the establishment of the 
SSM, much of the relevant information is stored in unstructured narr ative fields, making 
systematic analysis challenging. 
To overcome this challenge, we apply large language models (LLMs) to transform supervisory 
narratives into structured analytical variables. We first classify supervisory findings and 
measures into thematic categories using a dedicated taxonomy framework. We then construct 
a novel measure-level indicator of supervisory effectiveness by analysing supervisory closure 
narratives and classifying measures according to whether they resulted in full, partial, or no 
remediation of the underlying deficiency. This approach allows us to move beyond traditional 
process-based measures of supervision and towards an outcome -oriented assessment of 
supervisory effectiveness. 
Our analysis focuses on 8,1 06 credit-risk-related supervisory measures issued and closed 
between 2016 and 2025. Using the LLM -based effectiveness indicator, we examine which 
characteristics of supervisory measures, findings, and supervised institutions are associated 
with successful remediation in a logistic regression framework. We then analyse the duration 
of fully effective measures to identify the factors associated with faster or slower remediation 
using Cox proportional hazards model. 
Three main findings emerge. First, finding complexity is an important determinant of 
supervisory outcomes. Measures addressing multiple issues are less likely to achieve full 
remediation and remain open for longer periods. Data, reporting, and IT -related deficiencies 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
5
 
 
also prove particularly difficult to remediate. Second, supervisory measures arising from on -
site inspections exhibit higher remediation rates and shorter remediation periods than 
measures originating from broader supervisory processes such as the SREP or ongoing 
supervisory monitoring. Third, bank characteristics matter, albeit to a lesser extent than finding 
and measure characteristics. Stronger governance and greater profitability are associated with 
better remediation outcomes, although these relationsh ips weaken once supervisory -team 
heterogeneity is considered. 
This paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it provides one of the first large -
scale empirical assessments of supervisory effectiveness at the level of individual supervisory 
measures rather than supervisory frameworks or instruments. Se cond, it introduces a novel 
outcome-based measure of supervisory effectiveness grounded in the remediation of identified 
deficiencies. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence can be used to extract policy -
relevant information from large volumes of confidential supervisory text, thereby expanding the 
scope for empirical research and policy evaluation in banking supervision. 
The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on 
supervisory effectiveness and textual analysis. Section 3 describes the methodology and the 
construction of the LLM-based effectiveness indicator. Section 4 presents the data. Section 5 
discusses the empirical results. Section 6 concludes. 
2. Literature review 
This study draws on two strands of research. The first is the empirical literature on the 
effectiveness of banking supervision, reviewed in Section 2.1. The second is the literature on 
textual data and artificial intelligence in economics and finance, reviewed in Section 2.2. This 
paper is at the intersection of the two : a granular, measure -level assessment of supervisory 
effectiveness, made possible by applying large language models to a large body of 
unstructured supervisory text. 
2.1 Evaluating supervisory effectiveness 
The most comprehensive recent survey of this field is the Basel Committee's literature review 
on supervisory effectiveness (BCBS, 2025). It organises the evidence around a 'house of 
effectiveness': a set of enablers and impediments at the base, three pilla rs: risk identification 
and assessment, remediation and enforcement, and collaboration and transparency and 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
6
 
 
supervisory culture as the roof. This section follows that structure, after first setting out what 
effectiveness means and why it is hard to measure. 
2.1.1 Risk identification and assessment 
The first pillar concerns the tools through which supervisors identify and assess risk: on -site 
inspections, supervisory stress tests, horizontal reviews and benchmarking, and early-warning 
models (BCBS, 2025). On -site inspections have received the most em pirical attention, 
because they are intrusive and may involve a detailed review of the loan book. The Basel 
Committee's review reports that inspections promote more conservative risk management, 
with more prudent provisioning afterwards, and that the supervisory ratings derived from them 
have predictive power for financial stress (BCBS, 2025). Consistent with this, Passalacqua et 
al. (2021) use the quasi-random selection of Italian banks for inspection and find that inspected 
banks are more likely to reclassify loans as non-performing, cut credit to unproductive 'zombie' 
firms, and reallocate lending towards more productive borrowers, with positive spillovers for 
the wider economy; they trace these effects to improvements in bank governance. Bonfim et 
al. (2023) report comparable results for inspections of the largest Portuguese banks, although 
in that case the effect was confined to the inspected portfolios. Importantly, supervisory 
activities often extend beyond risk identification and contribute directly to remediation. The 
distinction between assessing weaknesses and ensuring their correction is therefore not 
always clear-cut. 
2.1.2 Remediation and enforcement 
The second pillar concerns the tools through which supervisors ensure that banks correct 
identified weaknesses and comply with prudential requirements. These include capital 
constraints under Pillar 2, enforcement and sanction actions, early -intervention regimes, and 
individual accountability regimes (BCBS, 2025). For a study focused on credit risk, the 
evidence on sanctions is particularly relevant. The Basel Committee's working paper finds that 
enforcement actions promote a more truthful classification of credit quality, reduce bank risk 
and lending, and generate deterrent effects on non -sanctioned banks, with effectiveness 
increasing in severity and depending critically on timing (BCBS, 2025). 
Prior studies find that supervisory sanctions and capital -related supervisory measures can 
reduce risk-taking and strengthen resilience, although their effectiveness depends on timing, 
severity and institutional context (Delis et al., 2016; Caiazza et al., 2018; Berger et al., 2022; 
BCBS, 2025). This literature is the closest precedent for the present study, yet a gap remains. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
7
 
 
Each of these studies measures the response of the bank, or of credit supply, to an 
enforcement tool. None measures whether a specific supervisory measure was implemented, 
and the underlying shortcoming rectified. Whether a measure achieves its purpose is unlikely 
to be uniform: a narrowly targeted measure may be more readily remedied than a broad one, 
and a bank with stronger governance, may comply more readily than a weaker peer. 
These remain conjectures because the evidence does not reach the level of the individual 
measure. As a result, little is known about which categories of findings are remediated, which 
are not, and which characteristics of banks and supervisory measures dis tinguish the two 
outcomes. 
Other dimensions of supervisory effectiveness, including coordination, transparency, 
consistency and supervisory culture, have also received attention in the literature. For 
example, Agarwal et al. (2014) show that differences in supervisory practices acro ss 
authorities can lead to inconsistent regulatory outcomes, while the BCBS (2025) highlights the 
roles of supervisory cooperation, transparency and organisational culture in supporting 
effective oversight. These dimensions are important determinants of supervisory outcomes but 
are less directly related to the measure-level focus of this paper. 
Taken together, the literature shows that the effectiveness of supervision depends on the tools 
used, on the bank, and on the institutional setting. What it does not provide is evidence at the 
level of the individual measure and its remediation . The binding constraint is not a lack of 
observations, but their form and confidentiality: the relevant information is recorded as free text 
rather than structured data and is typically not publicly accessible. This limitation is therefore 
less about data availability than about the ability to analyse them systematically. Turning 
unstructured supervisory text into analysable variables, and so into outcome-level evidence, is 
the methodological problem addressed in the next section. 
2.2 Textual analysis and artificial intelligence 
A key reason why effectiveness remains difficult to assess is that some of the richest 
supervisory records are stored as free text, inspection reports, findings, and the narratives that 
justify supervisory decisions , which conventional statistical methods cannot readily exploit. 
Advances in textual analysis, particularly through artificial intelligence, make it possible to 
convert this information into structured data, thereby enabling large-scale empirical analysis of 
supervisory outcomes that would otherwise be prohibitively time -consuming. Text-as-data 
approaches have become increasingly common in economics and finance, enabling 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
8
 
 
researchers to extract information from large collections of documents that would otherwise be 
difficult to analyse systematically (Gentzkow et al., 2019). 
Early applications relied primarily on dictionary -based approaches, which classify text using 
predefined word lists. While useful, these methods often struggle to capture context -specific 
meanings in financial and supervisory language (Loughran and McDonal d, 2011). More 
recently, machine learning techniques and large language models (LLMs) have substantially 
expanded the scope of textual analysis by allowing information to be interpreted in context and 
classified with greater flexibility (Huang et al., 2023; BIS, 2024; Korinek, 2023). 
These methods are increasingly being applied to central banking and financial stability 
analysis. Studies have shown that textual information contained in central bank publications 
can provide useful signals regarding perceptions of risk and future financi al vulnerabilities 
(Correa et al., 2021). Recent work at the ECB further demonstrates the potential of LLMs to 
identify and quantify risk assessments in financial stability communication and related policy 
documents (Fell et al., 2026). Applications to supervisory records remain comparatively limited, 
largely because such information is confidential. One notable exception is Goldsmith-Pinkham, 
Hirtle and Lucca (2016), who analyse the content of US supervisory examination reports and 
show that supervisory narratives contain information beyond formal supervisory ratings. 
However, existing studies have generally focused on characterising supervisory 
communication rather than assessing the outcomes of supervisory actions.

The two strands reviewed above leave a specific gap. While the supervisory effectiveness 
literature provides evidence on the impact of broad supervisory tools, it rarely assesses 
whether individual measures lead to the remediation of underlying deficiencies . This reflects 
the distinction between supervisory outputs, i.e. completed supervisory actions, and 
supervisory outcomes, i.e. effective remediation. At the same time, textual -analysis methods 
have rarely been applied to the outcomes of confidential supervisory actions. 
Using confidential supervisory data from ECB Banking Supervision, we apply large language 
models to identify whether individual measures resulted in full, partial or no remediation. This 
allows an outcome-oriented assessment of supervisory effectiveness at the measure level and 
provides evidence on the characteristics of supervisory measures and banks associated with 
more effective remediation outcomes.

be interpreted as a direct indicator of supervisory effectiveness.

Finding characteristics: The number of topics addressed within a measure is negatively 
associated with the speed of closure. Measures covering multiple topics require significantly 
longer remediation periods, suggesting that more complex findings are inherently more difficult 
to r esolve. This result is consistent with the notion that addressing several interconnected 
deficiencies often requires broader organisational changes, greater coordination across 
business areas, and more extensive supervisory follow-up. 
The nature of the underlying deficiency also plays an important role. Measures related to Data, 
Reporting & IT exhibit the longest remediation periods, while all other finding categories are 
associated with significantly faster closure. In particular, Gove rnance & Controls, NPE & 
Collateral Management, and Credit Lifecycle Management findings tend to be resolved more 
quickly. Remediation actions involving data infrastructures, reporting frameworks, and IT 
systems frequently require substantial investments, system development, and implementation 
efforts across multiple functions. By contrast, corrective actions targeting governance 
arrangements, credit processes, provisioning practices, or collateral management can often 
be implemented within shorter timeframes, resulting in faster remediation. 
The results indicate that the originator of the supervisory process is an important determinant 
of remediation speed. Relative to measures stemming from on -site inspections (OSI), 
measures originating from the SREP, Horizontal analyses, and JST activities exhibit 
significantly lower closure hazards, implying longer remediation periods. One possible 
explanation is that findings arising from broader supervisory assessments often relate to more

part of the variation attributed to bank characteristics in the baseline specification reflects 
persistent differences across supervised institutions or supervisory teams.

6. Conclusion 
This paper provides a granular, outcome-oriented assessment of supervisory effectiveness by 
focusing on the remediation of supervisory measures in credit risk. Using a novel application 
of LLM to confidential supervisory data, it constructs a measure-level indicator of effectiveness. 
Further, using the subset of fully effectively closed measures, a duration analysis is conducted. 
Both analyses assess drivers using measure characteristics and bank -specific factors 
providing a comprehensive narrative about their influence on remediation outcomes. 
Finding issue : The results show that finding complexity is an important determinant of 
supervisory outcomes. Measures addressing a larger number of topics are less likely to 
achieve full remediation and take substantially longer to close. In addition, Data, Reporting & 
IT findings emerge as particularly challenging to remediate. Relative to other finding types, 
such measures display both lower remediation rates and longer remediation horizons, 
highlighting the implementation challenges associated with data quality, reporting frameworks 
and IT infrastructures. Findings originating from on -site inspections outperform those 
stemming from broader supervisory activities, such as the SREP and ongoing JST 
assessments, both in terms of remediation rates and closure times. 
Measure Characteristics: Supervisory measure characteristics are strongly associated with 
both effectiveness and remediation speed. More severe measures are less likely to achieve 
full remediation and require longer implementation periods. Recommendations are associated 
with a hig her likelihood of full remediation, although legal enforceability does not appear to 
influence remediation speed. Taken together, these findings suggest that the nature of the 
underlying deficiency, the supervisory tool employed, and the complexity of impl ementation 
are important correlates of supervisory outcomes. 
Bank characteristics : Bank characteristics play a more nuanced role. More profitable 
institutions and banks with greater credit -risk materiality display stronger remediation 
outcomes in the baseline specifications, although these relationships weaken once JST -
specific heterogen eity is considered. By contrast, weaker governance is consistently 
associated with a lower likelihood of full remediation. At the same time, among measures that 
are fully remediated, weaker-governance institutions tend to achieve closure more quickly, a

result that may reflect selection effects or supervisory prioritisation rather than a direct 
governance effect on remediation speed. 
Time and Temporal Trends: The results indicate that measures initiated in most years after 
2016 are more likely to achieve full remediation, with particularly strong improvements 
observed in recent years. This pattern is consistent with an increased supervisory focus on 
remediation and follow-up, including the introduction of dedicated escalation frameworks and 
supervisory guidance supporting the closure of findings. 
Policy Implications : The findings offer several actionable insights for supervisors and 
policymakers: 
Simplifying Complex Measures : The greater effectiveness of recommendations and on -site 
measures may suggest that simplifying the implementation of measures could improve 
compliance. Supervisors should focus on feasibility, particularly for less well -resourced or 
poorly governed institutions. 
Tailoring Supervisory Strategies: Supervisors should account for bank-specific characteristics, 
such as governance, when designing and enforcing measures. The findings suggest that 
remediation strategies may need to be tailored to the characteristics and implementation 
capacity of supervised institutions. 
More broadly, the paper demonstrates how artificial intelligence can support the systematic 
evaluation of supervisory outcomes by transforming large volumes of unstructured supervisory 
information into empirically usable data. While the analysis identifies associations rather than 
causal effects and relies on documented remediation captured in supervisory narratives, it 
provides a practical framework for monitoring supervisory effectiveness at scale and 
contributes new evidence to the growing policy discussion on how supervisory success should 
be measured.

Cybersécurité des collectivités territoriales : la CNIL prononce dix sanctions
09 novembre 2026
En novembre 2026, la CNIL a prononcé dix sanctions simplifiées à l’encontre de collectivités territoriales et d’un établissement public, pour des manquements relatifs à la cybersécurité.
Le contexte
Les collectivités territoriales (communes, départements, régions) traitent un grand nombre de données, pour certaines sensibles (gestion de l’état civil des usagers, versement de prestations sociales, données financières, ou encore données concernant des mineurs).
C’est pourquoi, face au nombre croissant de cyberattaques, la CNIL a décidé, en 2025, de faire de la cybersécurité des collectivités territoriales l’une de ses thématiques annuelles de contrôle.
Plusieurs collectivités territoriales, acteurs publics, ainsi que leurs prestataires, ont ainsi été contrôlés, afin de vérifier que les mesures de sécurité, techniques, organisationnelles et physiques, mises en œuvre pour protéger les données des administrés étaient suffisantes.
Les contrôles ont révélé plusieurs manquements au RGPD et à la loi Informatique et Libertés, entraînant dix sanctions financières dans le cadre de la procédure simplifiée.
Les manquements sanctionnés
Des manquements à la sécurité (article 32 du RGPD)
Les manquements relevés témoignent de la diversité des failles pouvant affecter la sécurité d’un système d’information.
Il a notamment été constaté que :
- les modalités d’authentification permettant aux agents des collectivités de se connecter à distance (notamment en télétravail) n’étaient pas suffisamment robustes, en particulier pour ceux disposant de privilèges élevés (absence d’authentification multifacteur pour les administrateurs) ;
- certains prestataires extérieurs (par exemple, des éditeurs de logiciels) pouvaient accéder au réseau des collectivités de manière permanente, sans y être autorisés au cas par cas, ou via des comptes partagés entre plusieurs salariés ;
- les mesures déployées afin de détecter les comportements anormaux étaient inefficaces (journalisation incomplète ou absence d’exploitation en temps réel ou à court terme des journaux) ;
- le cloisonnement du réseau était insuffisant, ce qui pouvait étendre l’impact d’une violation à plusieurs segments du réseau ;
- certains systèmes d’exploitation utilisés par des serveurs étaient obsolètes : ils n’étaient plus maintenus à jour par leur éditeur et ne bénéficiaient donc pas des correctifs de sécurité adéquats ;
- certains mots de passe utilisés étaient insuffisamment robustes, transmis en clair aux usagers ou stockés dans des conditions ne permettant pas de garantir leur confidentialité.
L’ensemble de ces manquements exposaient les données, parfois sensibles, des administrés à des risques de perte de confidentialité. Certaines des collectivités contrôlées ont d’ailleurs subi une ou plusieurs violations de données, qui auraient pu être évitées si les mesures adéquates avaient été prises.
Plusieurs décisions relèvent également que les systèmes d’information des collectivités, utilisés notamment pour échanger en ligne avec les administrés, ne faisaient pas l’objet d’une homologation de sécurité avant leur mise en service, alors que le référentiel général de sécurité (RGS) l’exige. Cette homologation, rendue obligatoire, permet aux autorités administratives d’assurer la mise en conformité de leur système d’information.
Un manquement à l’obligation d’effectuer une analyse d’impact (articles 35 du RGPD et 90 de la loi Informatique et Libertés)
Plusieurs collectivités ont été sanctionnées pour ne pas avoir réalisé d’analyse d’impact (AIPD) préalablement à la mise en œuvre de certains traitements qui présentent des risques élevés pour les droits et libertés des personnes.
C’est notamment le cas :
- des téléservices permettant aux parents de gérer les activités scolaires et extrascolaires de leurs enfants, puisqu’ils concernent à la fois des personnes vulnérables (les enfants) et des  (des coordonnées bancaires) ;
- des systèmes de installés sur la voie publique, qui constituent « une surveillance systématique à grande échelle d’une zone accessible au public ».
Ces analyses auraient permis aux collectivités d’évaluer les risques liés aux traitements en cause et de prendre les mesures de sécurité nécessaires.
Les sanctions prononcées
Des amendes allant de 3 000 € à 20 000 € (maximum légal pour ce type de procédure) ont été prononcées. Ces montants tiennent notamment compte du nombre de manquements relevés et de leur gravité, des catégories de données traitées (données de mineurs, coordonnées bancaires, etc.), du budget de chacune des collectivités et du nombre de personnes concernées. Ils tiennent également comptent des mesures prises pour se mettre en conformité.
La CNIL, qui consacre en 2026 la moitié de ses contrôles et actions répressives à la sécurité des données, poursuivra ses vérifications afin de s’assurer que les données, parfois sensibles, des administrés sont traitées dans des conditions de sécurité satisfaisantes par les collectivités territoriales et leurs prestataires. D’autres procédures sont actuellement en cours et pourraient mener, en cas de manquements, à des sanctions, des mises en demeure ou des rappels aux obligations.
En parallèle, la CNIL poursuit ses actions de sensibilisation et d’accompagnement des collectivités territoriales en matière de cybersécurité. Cette double action de contrôle et d’accompagnement s’inscrira également dans la préparation de l’entrée en application de la directive NIS2, en cours de transposition, qui met à la charge notamment des collectivités territoriales de nouvelles exigences en matière de sécurité informatique.

Cybersécurité: les secteurs "hautement critiques" bientôt inscrits dans la loi
Les députés vont examiner ce lundi 9 novembre le projet de loi relatif au renforcement de la cybersécurité. Le texte prévoit notamment une reconnaissance précise des secteurs "hautement critiques", établissant une liste d'entités essentielles et importantes qui devront s'astreindre à des obligations supplémentaires.
Après moult rebondissements et un retard qui vaut à la France d'être poursuivie devant la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne, les députés vont enfin examiner pour de bon le projet de loi relatif au renforcement de la cybersécurité et à la résilience des infrastructures critiques dans l'hémicycle. Et ce grâce au rejet du budget, qui a permis d'ouvrir un trou dans l'agenda parlementaire surchargé.
Attendu depuis plusieurs mois, le texte transpose plusieurs directives européennes, dont celle dite "NIS 2". Celle-ci vise à assurer un niveau élevé commun de cybersécurité dans l’ensemble de l'espace européen, alors que ce dernier est régulièrement victime de cyberattaques. En France, tout particulièrement, plusieurs administrations ont été victimes de fuites de données durant l'été. Plus récemment, une douzaine de pays européens, dont la France, ont été touchés par des cyberattaques visant des réfrigérateurs et congélateurs de supermarchés.
Cette fragilité illustre la nécessité de renforcer la prévention contre les menaces, susceptibles désormais de cibler l'ensemble du tissu social et économique. C'est justement l'objet de la directive NIS 2, qui élargit les domaines concernés par des obligations de protection en la matière.
De 6 à 18 secteurs régulés
Le nombre de secteurs d'activités régulés va passer de six à 17 secteurs, classés selon leur importance critique, directement inscrits dans la loi. Les dix secteurs hautement critiques pour le fonctionnement de l'économie sont les secteurs de l'énergie, des transports, des banques, des infrastructures des marchés financiers, de la santé, de la distribution d'eau potable, des eaux usées, de l'infrastructure numérique, et de la gestion des services des technologies de l'information et de la communication.
S'ajoutent huit secteurs critiques, qui sont les services postaux, la gestion des déchets, la production et le transport de produits chimiques, la fabrication et le transport d'aliments, la fabrication de certains équipements et produits et de certains services numériques. Un décret viendra préciser les modalités précises de cette typologie.
Une hausse des entités régulées
En parallèle, les entités régulées - qui doivent appliquer des obligations de sécurité - vont passer de 500 à près de 15 000. Là encore, elles se décomposent en deux catégories, selon des critères précis fixés par la loi. Les entités essentielles sont celles qui devront remplir les obligations les plus poussées. Il peut s'agir d'entreprises qui appartiennent à un secteur "hautement critique", dont les effectifs sont au moins de 250 personnes et dont le chiffre d'affaires annuel est supérieur à 50 millions d'euros, des administrations centrales, de 1 500 collectivités locales, de certains prestataires de services, des acteurs de la chaîne d'enregistrement, des services départementaux d'incendie et de secours... Ont en revanche été exclues, à ce stade, les entités relevant de la sécurité nucléaire, les parlementaires souhaitant que la France puisse exercer sa compétence exclusive en la matière.
Les entités importantes devront elles aussi remplir des mesures de cybersécurité, toutefois moins exigeantes que celles qui s'appliquent aux entités essentielles. Là encore, sont concernées certaines entreprises, des opérateurs de communications électroniques, certaines collectivités territoriales comme les communautés de communes, certains établissements publics de santé et services sociaux. Par ailleurs, le Premier ministre pourra à l'avenir désigner par arrêté toute autre entité qu'il juge utile d'être reconnue comme essentielle ou importante.
Le cyber-pompier de l'État, l'Anssi (Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d'information) sera chargé d'établir et de mettre à jour la liste des entités essentielles et importantes. Dans l'attente de la transposition de la directive NIS 2, l'Anssi a d'ores et déjà publié une version de travail du référentiel qui a pour vocation de devenir le socle de réglementation cyber. Il reprend quinze objectifs de sécurité obligatoires à atteindre aussi bien pour les entités importantes qu’essentielles, dont une obligation d'enregistrement, mais aussi une obligation de déclaration de fuites de données ou d'incident cyber important. Les entités essentielles devront respecter cinq objectifs supplémentaires. Un espace dédié NIS 2 a été mis en place sur le site de l'Anssi, listant mesures juridiques, techniques et organisationnelles qui devront être mises en œuvre.
En cas de manquement aux obligations de cybersécurité, les entités régulées s'exposeront à des sanctions. Celles-ci seront proportionnées aux manquements, et pourront durement toucher au portefeuille de ceux qui se seront soustraits à leurs obligations : la directive prévoit en effet que les sanctions pourront aller jusqu'à 10 millions d'euros ou 2 % du chiffre d'affaires mondial des entités essentielles, et 1,4 % des entités importantes. Il ne reste désormais plus qu'à attendre la promulgation de loi, certaines entreprises attendant d'être assurées de leur statut précis.

Cette fragilité illustre la nécessité de renforcer la prévention contre les menaces, susceptibles désormais de cibler l'ensemble du tissu social et économique. C'est justement l'objet de la directive NIS 2, qui élargit les domaines concernés par des obligations de protection en la matière.
Le nombre de secteurs d'activités régulés va passer de six à 17 secteurs, classés selon leur importance critique, directement inscrits dans la loi. Les dix secteurs hautement critiques pour le fonctionnement de l'économie sont les secteurs de l'énergie, des transports, des banques, des infrastructures des marchés financiers, de la santé, de la distribution d'eau potable, des eaux usées, de l'infrastructure numérique, et de la gestion des services des technologies de l'information et de la communication.
S'ajoutent huit secteurs critiques, qui sont les services postaux, la gestion des déchets, la production et le transport de produits chimiques, la fabrication et le transport d'aliments, la fabrication de certains équipements et produits et de certains services numériques. Un décret viendra préciser les modalités précises de cette typologie.
En parallèle, les entités régulées - qui doivent appliquer des obligations de sécurité - vont passer de 500 à près de 15 000. Là encore, elles se décomposent en deux catégories, selon des critères précis fixés par la loi. Les entités essentielles sont celles qui devront remplir les obligations les plus poussées. Il peut s'agir d'entreprises qui appartiennent à un secteur "hautement critique", dont les effectifs sont au moins de 250 personnes et dont le chiffre d'affaires annuel est supérieur à 50 millions d'euros, des administrations centrales, de 1 500 collectivités locales, de certains prestataires de services, des acteurs de la chaîne d'enregistrement, des services départementaux d'incendie et de secours... Ont en revanche été exclues, à ce stade, les entités relevant de la sécurité nucléaire, les parlementaires souhaitant que la France puisse exercer sa compétence exclusive en la matière.
Les entités importantes devront elles aussi remplir des mesures de cybersécurité, toutefois moins exigeantes que celles qui s'appliquent aux entités essentielles. Là encore, sont concernées certaines entreprises, des opérateurs de communications électroniques, certaines collectivités territoriales comme les communautés de communes, certains établissements publics de santé et services sociaux. Par ailleurs, le Premier ministre pourra à l'avenir désigner par arrêté toute autre entité qu'il juge utile d'être reconnue comme essentielle ou importante.
Le cyber-pompier de l'État, l'Anssi (Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d'information) sera chargé d'établir et de mettre à jour la liste des entités essentielles et importantes. Dans l'attente de la transposition de la directive NIS 2, l'Anssi a d'ores et déjà publié une version de travail du référentiel qui a pour vocation de devenir le socle de réglementation cyber. Il reprend quinze objectifs de sécurité obligatoires à atteindre aussi bien pour les entités importantes qu’essentielles, dont une obligation d'enregistrement, mais aussi une obligation de déclaration de fuites de données ou d'incident cyber important. Les entités essentielles devront respecter cinq objectifs supplémentaires. Un espace dédié NIS 2 a été mis en place sur le site de l'Anssi, listant mesures juridiques, techniques et organisationnelles qui devront être mises en œuvre.
En cas de manquement aux obligations de cybersécurité, les entités régulées s'exposeront à des sanctions. Celles-ci seront proportionnées aux manquements, et pourront durement toucher au portefeuille de ceux qui se seront soustraits à leurs obligations : la directive prévoit en effet que les sanctions pourront aller jusqu'à 10 millions d'euros ou 2 % du chiffre d'affaires mondial des entités essentielles, et 1,4 % des entités importantes. Il ne reste désormais plus qu'à attendre la promulgation de loi, certaines entreprises attendant d'être assurées de leur statut précis.
